title: The numbers at line ends
hook: track changes shows every word slipped in; the Granth's numbers do something like it
tomorrow: a ballad, a stair, a couplet: what kinds of poem are in there?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the center: the rahao, the line marked pause, where a hymn's meaning sits. Start at the center. And right beside the rahao, in the text, there's a number.
screen: `START AT THE CENTER.` → `BESIDE IT, A NUMBER.`

segments.voice: A shared document with track changes on: every word anyone adds shows up in color, every cut leaves a line through it. Nobody slips anything in quietly. Now look at the end of any verse in the Granth. A double upright stroke, and a number: one. The next verse, two. At the end of a hymn, two or three numbers can sit side by side. So, why all the numbers? Part of the answer is a map. Part of it is older than any document app.
screen: `TRACK CHANGES: NOTHING SLIPS IN.` → `A STROKE, A NUMBER: ONE, TWO.` → `WHY ALL THE NUMBERS?`

segments.voice: First, the map. Each verse closes with its number. At a hymn's end you may see the last verse's number, then the hymn's own number in its group, and in places a running count. The rahao carries a number too. So the numbers guide: where a verse stops, where the center is, where one hymn ends and the next begins. Second, the guard. When every verse and hymn is counted, a line slipped in or dropped out would show. Guru Amar Das, in the Anand, says in paraphrase that apart from the True Guru's, every other word is unripe. The Granth keeps its words, and the numbers help keep them. Now a neighbor, in its own words. Jewish tradition carries this same care. In Deuteronomy, in the 1917 JPS translation: "Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you." Shared ground: sacred words kept whole, nothing added, nothing taken away. And one honest difference. In Deuteronomy, Moses is speaking about God's commandments, words to be lived as law. In the Granth, the words being kept are the Gurus' hymns, sung, and honored by Sikhs as the Guru itself, with the counting built into the page. Something to tell a friend tonight: two traditions, in their own words, guard their scripture from even one extra line.
screen: `THE MAP: VERSE, CENTER, HYMN.` · `THE GUARD: NOTHING SLIPS IN.` · `DEUTERONOMY: YE SHALL NOT ADD.` · `SHARED CARE, HONEST DIFFERENCE.` · then, large: `THE NUMBERS GUIDE.`

segments.voice: Open any hymn and count its verses on your fingers, one finger for each number at a line's end. When you reach the last one, look at the numbers sitting side by side. Then breathe slowly, one breath for each verse you counted, and let the count carry you to the end of the sit.
The numbers at line ends: the numbers that close each verse and each hymn in the Granth, counting them like an index built into the page. The eighth word of the year.
screen: `THE NUMBERS AT LINE ENDS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Something to keep: the numbers guide, and they guard what they count. Eight of twenty, counted.

howItsDone: In the Guru Granth Sahib each verse ends with a number between double strokes, and each hymn closes with its own numbers; readers use them to find their place, and the fixed text is copied and printed without additions.

notes: v3 wisdom day. Question: why would a scripture number its own verses? Sikh answer: the numbers guide (verse, rahao, hymn) and guard (nothing added; the Anand calls every word but the True Guru's unripe).

Unity thread (Judaism neighbor): Deuteronomy 4:2, quoted from JPS 1917 ('Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you'; the KJV has the same clause). Shared ground: sacred words kept whole. Honest difference: in Deuteronomy Moses speaks of God's commandments, to be lived as law; in the Granth the kept words are the Gurus' sung hymns, honored as the Guru, with the counting built into the page. Confirm a Jewish reader finds this fair and unranked, and confirm the JPS wording.
Anand Sahib pauri 24 (Ang 920): 'satguru bina hor kachi hai bani', paraphrased as 'apart from the True Guru's, every other word is unripe'. Confirm Ang and paraphrase.

Numbering described loosely on purpose: 'the hymn's own number in its group, and in places a running count'. No counts or totals are stated. Confirm the description of closing numbers (e.g. ॥੪॥੧॥) is fair.
The script does not claim the numbers were added by any particular Guru or scribe.
Gurmukhi ਅਨੰਦ (in the Granth ਅਨੰਦੁ), ਰਹਾਉ, numerals ੧ ੨ ੩ ੪ and the sound-outs to be checked.
